patient.name: Kieran Doherty
patient.setting: Emergency Department, then the respiratory ward
patient.complaint: Sudden sharp right-sided chest pain and breathlessness while sitting at his desk
background: Smokes 10 cigarettes a day and cannabis at weekends
No lung disease, no regular medicines

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness in a tall thin young smoker (primary) or a COPD patient (secondary), and tension pneumothorax when the stem adds hypotension and tracheal deviation.

points: Kieran, 22, tall and thin, felt a **sudden stab** in his right chest.
Pain is sharp and **worse on breathing in**.
Breathless walking to the bus stop.
No cough, fever or leg swelling.

steps.lead: Kieran is the textbook **primary spontaneous** case: tall, thin, young, male, smoking tobacco and cannabis, no lung disease.

points: Right side: reduced expansion, **hyper-resonant** to percussion.

steps.lead: Sudden pleuritic pain, hyper-resonance and quiet breath sounds on one side: **air in Kieran's right pleural space**.

steps.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis for Kieran?
steps.r: No underlying lung disease, so **primary**. PE does not give hyper-resonance; pneumonia gives dullness and fever.

steps.title: What you find on the affected side
head: Sign
Pneumothorax
Pleural effusion
Consolidation

steps.lead: Kieran's trachea is central and his BP is normal, so this is **not tension**. Hypotension plus tracheal deviation away would be.

steps.title: Simple or tension?
nodes: Hypotension, trachea deviated away, raised JVP → tension
steps.caption: Haemodynamics and the trachea decide.

steps.text: In tension pneumothorax the trachea deviates **away** from the affected side. Deviation **towards** a side suggests collapse or pneumonectomy.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?': chest X-ray confirms and sizes a stable pneumothorax, CT if unclear, and none at all for tension (clinical diagnosis).

steps.q: Kieran is stable. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
steps.r: **Chest X-ray** shows the pleural line and lets you measure the rim, which directs treatment.

steps.lead: Kieran is stable, so he gets an X-ray. If he were in **tension**, you would decompress first and image later.

visual.title: Kieran's chest X-ray
visual.caption: Visible right pleural line with no lung markings beyond it; no mediastinal shift.

steps.text: Look for the **pleural line** and **absent lung markings** peripheral to it.

visual.title: Rim of air at the hilum
visual.label: Kieran 3.2 cm
visual.caption: Over 2 cm and symptomatic: he needs a procedure, not just observation.

steps.lead: Kieran's film is clear-cut. **CT chest** is for when the X-ray is unclear, e.g. a large bulla in COPD.
Kieran's 3.2 cm rim is judged against the **BTS 2 cm** threshold, which sets the treatment pathway.
If Kieran needs a drain, you check it is working by watching the fluid **swing** and looking for **bubbling**.

steps.text: Never send a hypotensive patient with a deviated trachea for an X-ray. **Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis.**

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': needle aspiration for a symptomatic or >2 cm primary, chest drain if aspiration fails or the patient is ≥50 with a smoking history or has lung disease, and needle decompression for tension.

steps.lead: Kieran's pneumothorax is **primary, symptomatic and >2 cm**, so the first step is **needle aspiration** with an 18-gauge cannula.

steps.title: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax
steps.caption: Kieran is on the third line.

points: Repeat X-ray: rim still **2.6 cm**; still breathless.

steps.q: Kieran's aspiration has failed. What is the next step?
o: Discharge with review in 2 to 4 days
steps.r: A symptomatic pneumothorax >2 cm not resolved by aspiration needs a **chest drain**. Decompression is only for tension.

steps.lead: Kieran gets a **chest drain**. Older smokers, lung disease or instability would have earned one straight away.

visual.title: Kieran's rim of air
visual.caption: Bubbling stops by day 3 and the lung is up, so the drain comes out.

steps.lead: The drain is not allowed to suck Kieran's lung up too fast (**re-expansion oedema**), and **stopping smoking** is the biggest step against recurrence.
Had Kieran's drain kept **bubbling** past 3 to 5 days, or if he has a recurrence, he would go to cardiothoracic surgery for **VATS**.
If Kieran had become hypotensive with a deviated trachea, he would need **needle decompression** at once, before any X-ray.

steps.text: Tension: **16-gauge cannula**, **2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line** (or 5th ICS anterior axillary line), on the affected side, opposite the tracheal deviation. Then a chest drain.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why air in the pleura collapses the lung, why tension causes obstructive shock, or why tall thin people rupture apical blebs.

steps.lead: Kieran's height puts more **mechanical stress on his lung apex**, where a small subpleural **bleb** ruptured.
Air leaked into his pleural space and abolished the **negative intrapleural pressure** holding his right lung open.

steps.title: Tension pneumothorax
nodes: One-way valve: air in on inspiration, cannot leave
Pleural pressure rises with every breath
Mediastinum pushed to the other side
Great veins compressed: venous return falls

steps.lead: Kieran never developed this **one-way valve**; decompression would turn a tension into a simple pneumothorax.

steps.q: Why does tension pneumothorax cause hypotension?
o: Reduced venous return from compressed great veins
steps.r: Rising pressure shifts the mediastinum and **compresses the great veins**, cutting preload: **obstructive shock**.

steps.lead: If Kieran's lung had been re-expanded too fast, **reperfusion injury** and leaky capillaries could have flooded it with oedema.

steps.text: Pneumothorax lowers the **V/Q ratio**: the collapsed lung is still perfused but not ventilated, so oxygen saturation falls.

mcq.q: Who classically gets a primary spontaneous pneumothorax?
mcq.r: **Tall, thin young males**, often smokers (including cannabis), with no lung disease.

mcq.q: Which is the most important cause of secondary pneumothorax?
mcq.r: **COPD** is the most important; pulmonary fibrosis gives more severe disease.

mcq.q: In tension pneumothorax, which way does the trachea deviate?
mcq.r: **Away** from the affected side, with hypotension and distended neck veins.

mcq.q: Which investigation confirms a stable pneumothorax?
mcq.r: **Chest X-ray**: pleural line and absent lung markings beyond it.

mcq.q: What does a 'swinging' chest drain tell you?
o: The drain is patent and in the pleural space
mcq.r: Swinging means the drain is **patent**. Persistent **bubbling** means an ongoing air leak.

mcq.q: Where is needle decompression performed for tension pneumothorax?
mcq.r: **2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line** (or 5th ICS anterior axillary line), 16-gauge cannula.

mcq.q: Which is first-line for a symptomatic primary pneumothorax >2 cm?
mcq.r: **Needle aspiration** with an 18-gauge cannula; chest drain if it fails.

mcq.q: Which patient should go straight to a chest drain?
mcq.r: **Age ≥50 with a significant smoking history** is a chest drain indication.

mcq.q: What is the risk of draining a large pneumothorax too quickly?
mcq.r: **Re-expansion pulmonary oedema** from reperfusion injury and leaky capillaries.

mcq.q: What is the mechanism of a tension pneumothorax?
mcq.r: A **one-way valve**: air enters on inspiration but cannot escape.

prompts.q: What is a pneumothorax and how does it present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: sudden, pleuritic, one-sided, hyper-resonant.

points.p: Air in the pleural cavity causing lung collapse
points.why: Between the visceral and parietal pleura.

points.p: Sudden-onset pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness
Hyper-resonant percussion on the affected side
points.why: Dullness means fluid or consolidation instead.

points.p: Reduced air entry / breath sounds
points.why: With reduced expansion on that side.

prompts.q: How do primary and secondary spontaneous pneumothoraces differ?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: any lung disease makes it secondary.

points.p: Primary: no lung disease, apical bleb rupture
Primary: tall, thin young males and smokers (including cannabis)
Secondary: underlying lung disease, most importantly COPD
points.why: Secondary needs a drain or inpatient monitoring.

points.p: Also pulmonary fibrosis (more severe), asthma, Marfan's, post chest drain

prompts.q: What are the features of a tension pneumothorax?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: shock + trachea away + hyper-resonant = decompress.

points.p: Hypotension / haemodynamic instability (obstructive shock)
points.why: The feature that separates it from simple pneumothorax.

points.p: Tracheal deviation away from the affected side
Absent breath sounds, hyper-resonance, reduced expansion, reduced vocal resonance
Distended neck veins, surgical emphysema, often after trauma
points.why: Raised JVP from obstructed venous return.

prompts.q: How do you tell pneumothorax from effusion and consolidation at the bedside?

points.p: Pneumothorax: hyper-resonant, reduced breath sounds
points.why: The only one that is hyper-resonant.

points.p: Effusion: stony dull, reduced breath sounds
points.why: Massive effusion also pushes the trachea away.

points.p: Consolidation: dull, bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance

prompts.q: How do you investigate a suspected pneumothorax, and when do you not?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: stable = X-ray; tension = no imaging.

points.p: Chest X-ray: pleural line with absent lung markings beyond it
points.why: Also sizes it against the 2 cm threshold.

points.p: CT chest if the diagnosis is unclear
Tension is a clinical diagnosis: treat before imaging

prompts.q: How do you check a chest drain is working?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: swing = patent; bubble = leak.

points.p: Fluid swinging with respiration = patent drain in the pleural space
points.why: No swing suggests a blocked, kinked or displaced drain.

points.p: Persistent bubbling in the water seal = ongoing air leak
points.why: Leak beyond 3 to 5 days: refer to surgeons.

prompts.q: How do you manage a primary spontaneous pneumothorax?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 2 cm and symptoms decide.

points.p: Asymptomatic, <2 cm: discharge, outpatient review in 2–4 days
points.why: Minimally symptomatic of any size can be managed conservatively.

points.p: Symptomatic and/or >2 cm: needle aspiration (18-gauge)
Aspiration fails: chest drain
Persistent air leak (3–5 days) or recurrence: cardiothoracic referral, VATS pleurodesis ± bullectomy
Smoking cessation

prompts.q: Who needs a chest drain straight away, and how do you treat a tension pneumothorax?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: age 50 + smoking = drain; tension = needle now.

points.p: Drain: age ≥50 with smoking history, underlying lung disease, bilateral
points.why: The 55 year old smoker with a 4 cm rim gets a drain.

points.p: Drain: haemodynamic compromise, significant hypoxia, haemothorax
Tension: immediate needle decompression with a 16-gauge cannula
2nd ICS mid-clavicular line (or 5th ICS anterior axillary line), opposite the tracheal deviation
points.why: 5th ICS mid-clavicular is the classic wrong option.

points.p: Small stable secondary: inpatient monitoring
points.why: Secondary is never sent straight home.

prompts.q: Why does a pneumothorax collapse the lung, and why do primary ones affect tall, thin people?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: negative pressure holds the lung open.

points.p: Air enters via a breach in the visceral or parietal pleura
points.why: Usually the visceral pleura in spontaneous cases.

points.p: Loss of negative intrapleural pressure lets the lung recoil and collapse
points.why: Elastic recoil pulls the lung in.

points.p: Rupture of a subpleural apical bleb or bulla
Tall, thin people have greater mechanical stress at the apex

prompts.q: Why does tension pneumothorax cause shock, and why can rapid re-expansion cause oedema?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one-way valve, then no venous return.

points.p: One-way valve: air enters on inspiration but cannot escape
Mediastinal shift compresses the great veins and heart
Decompression converts tension to simple pneumothorax
Re-expansion oedema: reperfusion injury and increased capillary permeability

glossary.pneumothorax: Air in the pleural space, between the lung and chest wall, causing the lung to collapse.
glossary.primary spontaneous pneumothorax: Pneumothorax with no underlying lung disease, usually from an apical bleb in a tall thin young man.
glossary.secondary spontaneous pneumothorax: Pneumothorax caused by underlying lung disease such as COPD.
glossary.tension pneumothorax: Life-threatening pneumothorax where trapped air builds pressure, shifts the mediastinum and causes shock.
glossary.pleural cavity: The thin space between the visceral pleura on the lung and the parietal pleura on the chest wall.
glossary.visceral pleura: The membrane covering the lung surface.
glossary.parietal pleura: The membrane lining the inside of the chest wall.
glossary.pleural line: The thin white edge of the collapsed lung seen on a chest X-ray.
glossary.pleuritic: Sharp chest pain that is worse on breathing in or coughing.
glossary.hyper-resonant: A hollow, drum-like percussion note over air, as in pneumothorax.
glossary.vocal resonance: How clearly spoken sounds transmit through the chest; reduced over air or fluid.
glossary.bleb: A small air-filled blister under the visceral pleura, usually at the lung apex.
glossary.bulla: An air space larger than 1 cm within the lung, common in emphysema.
glossary.COPD: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; the most important cause of secondary pneumothorax.
glossary.Marfan's: Inherited connective tissue disorder causing tall stature and a higher risk of pneumothorax.
glossary.obstructive shock: Shock from blocked venous return or cardiac filling, as in tension pneumothorax.
glossary.mediastinal shift: Movement of the heart and trachea away from a high-pressure side of the chest.
glossary.tracheal deviation: The trachea pushed off the midline; away from the side of a tension pneumothorax.
glossary.surgical emphysema: Air trapped under the skin, felt as crackling (crepitus).
glossary.crepitus: A crackling feeling under the fingers from air in the tissues.
glossary.V/Q ratio: Ventilation to perfusion ratio; falls when collapsed lung is still perfused.
glossary.needle aspiration: Removing air from the pleural space through a cannula; first-line for symptomatic primary pneumothorax.
glossary.needle decompression: Emergency cannula into the chest to release trapped air in tension pneumothorax.
glossary.needle thoracocentesis: Another name for needle decompression of the chest.
glossary.intercostal space: The gap between two ribs; the 2nd is used for needle decompression.
glossary.mid-clavicular line: A vertical line down from the middle of the clavicle.
glossary.anterior axillary line: A vertical line down from the front fold of the armpit.
glossary.chest drain: A tube inserted into the pleural space, connected to an underwater seal, to let air or fluid out.
glossary.underwater seal: Drain bottle where the tube sits under water so air escapes but cannot return.
glossary.swinging: Drain fluid moving up and down with breathing, showing the drain is patent.
glossary.bubbling: Air bubbles in the water seal, showing an ongoing air leak.
glossary.air leak: Continued escape of air from the lung into the pleural space.
glossary.VATS: Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery: keyhole chest surgery for pleurodesis or bullectomy.
glossary.pleurodesis: Sticking the pleural layers together mechanically or chemically to prevent recurrence.
glossary.re-expansion pulmonary oedema: Fluid in a lung that has been re-expanded too quickly after collapse.
glossary.BTS: British Thoracic Society, which publishes the UK pneumothorax guidelines.
glossary.16-gauge: Large-bore cannula size used for needle decompression.

technique.stem: A 33 year old tall man is brought to the Emergency Department severely breathless. His pulse rate is 132 bpm, BP 78/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 84% on 15 L oxygen. His trachea is deviated to the right. There are no breath sounds and reduced expansion on the left, which is hyper-resonant. His neck veins are distended.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question in a shocked, breathless patient: examine the chest signs.

clues: trachea is deviated to the right
no breath sounds and reduced expansion on the left
steps.x: Shock, trachea pushed **away** from the silent, hyper-resonant left side, raised JVP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Left tension pneumothorax.**

elim: Asthma is bilateral wheeze, without tracheal deviation.
Tamponade gives muffled heart sounds with normal, symmetrical breath sounds.
An effusion is dull, not hyper-resonant.
Massive PE causes shock but a clear, symmetrical chest.

steps.x: **E. Tension pneumothorax.** Rule: shock + trachea away + hyper-resonant silent side = tension.

technique.stem: A 26 year old man had a right chest drain inserted for a pneumothorax 6 hours ago. The water seal shows no bubbling and the fluid level does not move with breathing or coughing. He is more breathless. His pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most likely explanation of the drain findings?
o: Drain is blocked, kinked or displaced
Lung has fully re-expanded and he is improving

steps.x: A drain-assessment question: interpret swinging and bubbling.

clues: does not move with breathing or coughing
steps.x: No **swing** and he is worse: the drain is not working.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Blocked, kinked or displaced drain.**

elim: A working drain swings with respiration.
A re-expanded lung can reduce the swing, but he would be improving, not more breathless.
An air leak shows persistent bubbling; there is none.
Re-expansion oedema follows over-rapid re-expansion; the drain findings point to failure instead.

steps.x: **B. Drain not working.** Rule: swing = patent; no swing + worse = blocked or displaced.

technique.stem: A 24 year old man has had a right chest drain for a primary spontaneous pneumothorax for 5 days. The drain is still bubbling continuously and the repeat chest X-ray shows the lung has not fully re-expanded. His pulse rate is 84 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Remove the drain and repeat aspiration

steps.x: Next step when a drain has failed.
**Persistent air leak** and failed re-expansion beyond 3 to 5 days.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Refer to **cardiothoracic surgery** (VATS pleurodesis ± bullectomy).

elim: Another drain does not fix the leak; surgery does.
Decompression is for tension; he is stable.
Aspiration has a lower success rate than a drain already in place.
He cannot go home with an unresolved air leak.

steps.x: **C. Cardiothoracic referral.** Rule: leak beyond 3 to 5 days = surgeons (VATS).

technique.stem: A 19 year old man who is 1.95 m tall and very thin has a sudden left-sided pleuritic chest pain while studying. He smokes cannabis. He has no lung disease. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg. Chest X-ray shows a left apical pneumothorax.
technique.q: Which is the most likely underlying mechanism?
o: Bronchial obstruction by a mucus plug
Rupture of a subpleural apical bleb
Rupture of an emphysematous bulla from COPD

steps.x: A mechanism question for a primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
Tall, thin, young, no lung disease: **primary**. Apical stress ruptures a **bleb**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Subpleural apical bleb rupture.**

elim: A mucus plug causes collapse without pleural air.
There is no infection described.
No trauma is described.
COPD bullae cause secondary pneumothorax in older smokers.

steps.x: **D. Apical bleb rupture.** Rule: tall thin young man = bleb, primary pneumothorax.

practice.stem: A 20 year old man has a 2 hour history of sudden right-sided chest pain, worse on inspiration, and breathlessness. He is tall and thin and smokes. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. There is reduced air entry and hyper-resonance on the right. His trachea is central.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sudden pleuritic pain with right-sided hyper-resonance and reduced air entry in a tall, thin young smoker is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax. Normal BP and a central trachea exclude tension.

steps.x: Diagnosis of sudden pleuritic chest pain.

clues: sudden right-sided chest pain, worse on inspiration
steps.x: Classic habitus, **hyper-resonance**, stable, trachea central.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Primary spontaneous pneumothorax.**

elim: Costochondritis gives chest wall tenderness with a normal chest examination.
Pneumonia gives fever and dullness, not hyper-resonance.
PE causes pleuritic pain but a normal percussion note.
Tension needs shock and tracheal deviation; he is stable.

steps.x: **C. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax.** Rule: tall thin young smoker + hyper-resonance = primary.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman with COPD has a sudden increase in breathlessness and left-sided chest pain. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86% breathing air. Breath sounds are reduced on the left. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Left pleural line with absent lung markings beyond it; hyperexpanded lungs.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A pneumothorax in a patient with COPD is secondary, because there is underlying lung disease. It is more dangerous and always needs admission. Primary pneumothorax means no lung disease.

steps.x: Diagnosis: the X-ray shows air; the history classifies it.

clues: Breath sounds are reduced on the left
steps.x: Sudden worsening, one-sided signs, pleural line on X-ray, known **COPD**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.**

elim: An exacerbation does not show a pleural line.
Pneumonia shows consolidation and fever.
Primary means no underlying lung disease.
PE does not produce a pleural line on X-ray.

steps.x: **E. Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.** Rule: pneumothorax + lung disease = secondary.

practice.stem: A 31 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department after a stab wound to the left chest. His pulse rate is 136 bpm, BP 74/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 82% on 15 L oxygen. His trachea is deviated to the right. The left chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds. Heart sounds are clearly audible.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Trauma, shock, tracheal deviation away from a hyper-resonant silent side is tension pneumothorax. Haemothorax would be dull; tamponade gives muffled heart sounds.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a shocked trauma patient.

clues: stab wound to the left chest
trachea is deviated to the right
steps.x: Shock, trachea **away**, **hyper-resonant**, normal heart sounds.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Left tension pneumothorax.**

elim: Tamponade gives muffled heart sounds and a normal chest note.
Flail chest shows paradoxical movement of a chest segment.
Haemothorax is dull to percussion.
A simple pneumothorax does not cause shock or tracheal deviation.

steps.x: **E. Tension pneumothorax.** Rule: hyper-resonant + shock + trachea away = tension.

practice.stem: A 25 year old woman has a 3 hour history of sudden left-sided pleuritic chest pain. She is breathless on walking. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows a left pneumothorax with a 2.5 cm rim and no mediastinal shift.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the left chest?
practice.e: Air in the pleural space gives a hyper-resonant percussion note with reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance. Stony dullness is an effusion; bronchial breathing is consolidation.

steps.x: An examination finding for a confirmed pneumothorax.
Simple left pneumothorax.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hyper-resonance**, reduced breath sounds.

elim: Bronchial breathing is consolidation.
Crackles suggest fluid in alveoli or fibrosis.
Vocal resonance is reduced over air, increased over consolidation.
Stony dullness is a pleural effusion.

steps.x: **C. Hyper-resonant.** Rule: air = hyper-resonant; fluid = dull.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man has sudden right-sided chest pain and breathlessness. He has a 50 pack-year smoking history, a chronic productive cough and a barrel-shaped chest. His pulse rate is 108 bpm, BP 136/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows a right pneumothorax and hyperexpanded lungs.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his pneumothorax?
o: Rupture of an apical bleb in healthy lung
practice.e: A heavy smoker with a barrel chest and obstructive spirometry has COPD, the most important cause of secondary pneumothorax. Apical bleb rupture in healthy lung is the primary mechanism in young people.

steps.x: A cause question: identify the underlying lung disease.
Smoker, chronic cough, hyperexpansion, FEV1/FVC 0.52: **COPD**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **COPD**, causing a secondary pneumothorax.

elim: Asthma is reversible and less likely at 62 with this smoking history.
IPF gives a restrictive pattern and small lungs.
Marfan's presents young with tall stature.
His lungs are not healthy: this is secondary, not primary.

steps.x: **B. COPD.** Rule: COPD is the most important cause of secondary pneumothorax.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man had a chest drain inserted for a large right pneumothorax 1 hour ago, with rapid drainage on suction. He now has a cough with frothy pink sputum and worsening breathlessness. His pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 87% on 4 L oxygen. Repeat X-ray shows the right lung re-expanded with new right-sided airspace shadowing.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Frothy sputum and new shadowing confined to the just re-expanded lung after rapid drainage is re-expansion pulmonary oedema. Left ventricular failure would be bilateral.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a complication after drainage.

clues: re-expanded with new right-sided airspace shadowing
steps.x: Over-rapid re-expansion, then oedema **only on that side**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Re-expansion pulmonary oedema.**

elim: Aspiration needs a reason to aspirate and takes longer to develop.
Haemothorax shows fluid and dullness, not frothy sputum.
LVF gives bilateral oedema, not one-sided.
The lung has re-expanded; tension would show collapse and shock.

steps.x: **D. Re-expansion pulmonary oedema.** Rule: rapid drainage + one-sided oedema = re-expansion.

practice.stem: A 23 year old man has a 4 hour history of sudden left-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild breathlessness. His pulse rate is 92 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. There is reduced air entry and hyper-resonance on the left. His trachea is central.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: A stable suspected pneumothorax is confirmed with a chest X-ray, which also measures the rim to guide treatment. CT is only needed if the X-ray is unclear.

steps.x: Initial investigation in a stable patient.
Stable, suspected simple pneumothorax.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chest X-ray.**

elim: An ABG does not confirm a pneumothorax; his saturations are normal.
CTPA is for PE; hyper-resonance points to air.
D-dimer is for PE risk assessment.
Echo is for tamponade or heart failure.

steps.x: **B. Chest X-ray.** Rule: stable = CXR to confirm and size; tension = no imaging.

practice.stem: A 71 year old man with severe emphysema has increased breathlessness. His pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. His chest X-ray shows a large lucent area in the right upper zone with no clear pleural line; the radiologist cannot tell a large bulla from a pneumothorax.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: CT chest is used when the X-ray is unclear, such as telling a large bulla from a pneumothorax in emphysema. Putting a drain into a bulla would be dangerous.

steps.x: Next investigation when the first-line test is inconclusive.

clues: cannot tell a large bulla from a pneumothorax
steps.x: X-ray **inconclusive** in bullous lung disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT chest.**

elim: Bronchoscopy looks at airways, not the pleura.
A lateral film rarely settles bulla versus pneumothorax.
Spirometry measures airflow, not pleural air.
A V/Q scan is for PE.

steps.x: **B. CT chest.** Rule: CXR unclear = CT chest.

practice.stem: A 27 year old man has right-sided chest pain and breathlessness of sudden onset over the past 2 hours. He has no lung disease. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 120/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows a right pneumothorax with a 3.5 cm rim of air and no mediastinal shift.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Discharge with outpatient review in 2 to 4 days
Needle decompression in the 2nd intercostal space
practice.e: A symptomatic primary pneumothorax with a rim over 2 cm is treated first with needle aspiration. A chest drain is second-line if aspiration fails; decompression is for tension only.

steps.x: Initial management: classify, then size.
Young, **primary**, symptomatic, **>2 cm**, stable, not tension.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Needle aspiration.**

elim: Discharge is for asymptomatic primary pneumothorax under 2 cm.
A drain is second-line, or first-line if over 50 with smoking or lung disease.
Decompression is for tension; he is stable with no shift.
VATS is third-line, for persistent leak or recurrence.

steps.x: **C. Needle aspiration.** Rule: primary + symptomatic or >2 cm = aspirate first.

practice.stem: A 56 year old man has sudden left-sided chest pain and breathlessness for 1 hour. He is usually well but smokes 30 cigarettes a day. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 86 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows a left pneumothorax with a 4 cm rim. There is no mediastinal shift.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Needle decompression in the 2nd intercostal space
practice.e: Age 50 or over with a significant smoking history is an indication for a chest drain rather than aspiration. Decompression is for tension, and VATS is for persistent leak or recurrence.

steps.x: Initial management: look for chest drain indications.
**≥50 with a smoking history**, large, symptomatic, not tension.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chest drain.**

elim: Oxygen alone is for small, minimally symptomatic pneumothoraces.
He is symptomatic with a large pneumothorax.
No tension: BP is normal and there is no shift.
VATS is third-line.

steps.x: **C. Chest drain.** Rule: age ≥50 + smoking = drain, not aspiration.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department severely breathless after a fall from a ladder. His pulse rate is 138 bpm, BP 76/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 80% on 15 L oxygen. His trachea is deviated to the left. The right chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds and his neck veins are distended.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Needle decompression, left 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line
Needle decompression, right 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line
Needle decompression, right 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line
Right chest drain after a chest X-ray
practice.e: A right tension pneumothorax needs immediate needle decompression with a 16-gauge cannula in the right 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line, opposite the tracheal deviation. Imaging must not delay it.

steps.x: Immediate management in a shocked patient: side and site both matter.

clues: trachea is deviated to the left
right chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds
steps.x: **Right tension pneumothorax**: trachea pushed left.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Right** 2nd ICS mid-clavicular needle decompression now.

elim: Wrong side: decompress the affected side, opposite the tracheal deviation.
5th ICS mid-clavicular is the wrong site (5th ICS is anterior axillary).
A drain follows decompression; waiting for an X-ray wastes time.
Tension is a clinical diagnosis; do not image first.

steps.x: **B. Right 2nd ICS MCL decompression.** Rule: tension = decompress the side opposite the deviation, now.

practice.stem: A 29 year old man with a right pneumothorax deteriorates while waiting for a chest drain. His pulse rate rises to 140 bpm, BP falls to 70/40 mmHg and his neck veins become distended. His trachea shifts to the left.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hypotension?
o: Hypovolaemia from blood loss into the pleura
Reduced venous return from raised intrathoracic pressure
practice.e: A one-way valve traps air, raising intrathoracic pressure, shifting the mediastinum and compressing the great veins, so venous return and cardiac output fall: obstructive shock. Hypovolaemia would give flat neck veins.

steps.x: A mechanism question about shock in tension pneumothorax.
Tension: **raised JVP** with shock means blood cannot get back to the heart.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Reduced venous return**: obstructive shock.

elim: Hypovolaemia gives flat, not distended, neck veins.
The heart is compressed, not intrinsically failing.
No infection; sepsis gives warm vasodilated shock.
He is tachycardic, not bradycardic.

steps.x: **D. Reduced venous return.** Rule: tension = obstructive shock with distended neck veins.
